newsitem.title: USA: Magellan boosts stocks, still losing assets.
newsitem.headline: Magellan boosts stocks, still losing assets.

text.p: The Magellan Fund shrank in February and has failed to outperform a widely watched market gauge, Fidelity Investments said Tuesday, as Robert Stansky tried to restore luster to the nation's largest mutual fund.
Fidelity said Magellan's stock holdings stood at 93.5 percent of assets as of Jan. 31, up from 89.6 percent a month earlier, and that its holdings in bonds and cash declined.
Despite Stansky's moves to turn Magellan around, investors pulled money from the giant fund. Magellan's net assets fell to $53.79 billion at Feb. 28 from $55.15 billion as of Jan. 31, Fidelity said.

Eric Kobren, editor of Fidelity Insight, a newsletter that tracks the giant mutual fund company, estimated Magellan lost about $630 million in net redemptions in February, compared with $1.2 billion in January.
Magellan's net outflows "have improved quite a bit, they're still negative but they've improved," Kobren said.
A mutual fund's total net assets reflect its investment performance and the flow of money in and out of the fund.

Since Stansky took the helm at the fund on June 1 from former manager Jeffrey Vinik, he has been shifting its assets from cash and bonds into stocks. Vinik's big bet on bonds in late 1995 was widely blamed for Magellan's dismal performance last year.

The Boston-based mutual fund company said in its monthly stock guide that Stansky cut bonds to 0.8 percent of Magellan's assets at Jan. 31 from 3.8 percent a month earlier. He reduced assets in cash to 5.7 percent from 6.6 percent.
But Magellan is still underperforming the Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks, a widely watched market barometer.
The S&P 500 was up 10.2 percent for the year as of Monday, the S&P index of 400 medium-sized stocks rose 5.1 percent and the Russell 2000 index of smaller stocks gained 1.5 percent, Kobren said.
Magellan is up to "6.1 percent which not as good as the S&P 500, but is better than the midcap and small cap performance," Kobren said.

Fidelity watcher David O'Leary of Alpha Equity Research, Inc. was less enthusiastic predicting that Vanguard's S&P500 fund, with $40 billion in assets, will soon overtake Magellan as the biggest fund because it is outperforming Stansky.
"Fidelity has had a drastic decline in market share of the mutual fund industry," O'Leary said. "Fidelity itself uses the S&P 500 index as the benchmark for Magellan."
He noted it has taken Stansky 10 months to bring the fund's portfolio "back to where it should have been, in stocks. And the question remains why has it taken him so long."
Fidelity said Magellan raised the percentage of holdings in the technology sector to 14.6 percent from 13.7 percent. It also boosted the health care sector to 6.3 percent from 4.9 percent.

General Motors Corp., one of Magellan's top 10 holdings at Dec. 31, was replaced by Citicorp at Jan. 31, Fidelity said. The top three holdings as of Jan. 31 remained Intel Corp., General Electric Co. and Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
"The fund is fairly well diversified. There's a bit of overweighting in technology and energy but he's not making any tremendous sector bets," Kobren said.
Stansky has "repositioned the fund where it will likely be in the long term," he added.
Kobren said Stansky had his work cut out for him.
"It is not going to blow away the averages, and it is not going to blow away the smaller more nimble competitors. It's just not going to do it."
